teaser: She is famous for what she lacks. Her missing arms hide a second secret: she was built in pieces.
review_notes:
Height 2.04 m is the Louvre figure (some sources give 2.02 m).
The statue is described as carved from two main blocks of Parian marble joined at the hips, with left arm and left foot added separately: standard account, please confirm wording.
The lost inscribed block naming '...andros son of Menides of Antioch on the Maeander' and the idea that its disappearance suited the Louvre's wish for a Classical date: widely reported, the motive is interpretation.
1964 loan to Japan (Tokyo and Kyoto) and wartime shelter at the Chateau de Valencay: to verify.
The two small holes pointed at on her right upper arm are read here as fixing holes for a metal armband; some scholars link them to an ancient repair or support instead.
Metadata year -120: the Louvre dates it about 150 to 125 BC, consistent.

lesson.text: Two meters and four centimeters of marble, about 6 feet 8 inches. If she stepped down from her base, she would look over the head of nearly everyone in the room. The Venus de Milo is not a life-size woman. She is a goddess, and she was carved larger than you on purpose.

The marble comes from Paros, a Greek island whose stone was prized because light sinks a little way into it before bouncing back, the way it does on skin. Around 150 to 125 BC, a sculptor used it for a temple or a gymnasium on the nearby island of Melos. “Milo” is simply a later spelling of that island's name.

A farmer digging for building stones in a ruin found her in April 1820. A young French naval officer happened to be nearby and sketched the pieces as they came out of the ground. Within a year she was a gift to King Louis XVIII, who passed her on to the Louvre.

“Pieces” is the right word. Greek sculptors of this period often did not carve a big figure from a single block. They built it, the way a carpenter builds furniture, from parts shaped separately and pinned together. The statue still shows where.

lesson.title: How she was assembled
lesson.text: Three places where the construction, and the damage, can still be read on the stone.

spots.title: The hidden seam
spots.text: The nude torso and the draped legs are two different blocks. They meet here, and the thick roll of cloth around the hips is there partly to disguise the joint.

spots.title: The left shoulder
spots.text: A flat, rough break. The left arm was a separate piece of marble, fixed into the shoulder with a peg. It was raised, which is why this shoulder sits higher than the other.

spots.title: The right arm
spots.text: It ends above the elbow. This arm crossed in front of her body, perhaps toward the cloth sliding off her left hip.

lesson.text: So the arms were always the fragile part: add-ons, held by metal pins that rust and loosen. A marble hand holding an apple was found near her, along with part of an upper arm. Many scholars think they belong to her. Others have imagined her spinning thread, or admiring herself in a polished shield. Nobody can prove it.
The Venus de Milo was assembled from separately carved blocks. The joins that made her possible are also the reason she came down to us incomplete.

Forget the arms for a moment and follow the body. She does not stand like a column. Her weight is on one leg, the other knee pushes forward under the cloth, and her head turns away from where her chest is facing. Each part answers the one below it with a small twist.
Three lines show how a standing figure can seem to be turning.

lines.label: The serpentine axis
lines.text: Trace the middle of the body from hair to foot and you get a slow S. This twist invites you to walk around her: no single viewpoint tells you everything.

lines.label: The dividing line
lines.text: The slanted edge of the drapery cuts her in two. Above it, calm polished skin. Below, deep restless folds that catch shadow.

lines.label: Her gaze
lines.text: She looks off to her left, past you. The calm, distant face borrows from statues made two centuries earlier, a deliberately old-fashioned touch.

lesson.text: That mix is the sculptor's real signature. The face is cool and remote, in the manner of the great Athenian sculptors of the 400s and 300s BC. The spiraling pose and the cloth about to slip are tastes of his own, later time, which historians call Hellenistic: the centuries after Alexander the Great, when Greek art turned more theatrical and sensual.

A block found with the statue carried a signature ending in “…andros, son of Menides, from Antioch on the Maeander.” It dated her to the later period, which was less prestigious at the time. The Louvre preferred to present her as an older classic, and the inscribed block went missing. It has never been found.

She was not always this bare, either. The marble was pierced so that real metal jewelry could be attached: earrings, a band in the hair, a bracelet. Like most ancient statues she was probably painted as well, though no color survives.
Two small drilled holes remain on one arm, where a metal armband may once have been fastened. Can you spot them?

spots.title: Fixing holes
spots.text: Two dark dots on her right upper arm, just beside the breast. Picture a band of gilded bronze here, glinting against painted skin: a very different goddess from the white one we know.

lesson.text: Why did this broken statue become the most famous sculpture in France? Timing helped. In 1815 the Louvre had to send back the artworks Napoleon had seized across Europe, including a celebrated Venus returned to Florence. Five years later a new Greek goddess arrived, and the museum promoted her with everything it had.

She has left the Louvre only a handful of times. During the Second World War she was packed in a crate and hidden in a château in the French countryside. In 1964 she traveled by ship to Japan, where enormous crowds lined up to see her.

Restorers of the 1820s thought about giving her new arms, as was normal then. They chose not to. It may be the best decision ever made about her: the empty space lets every visitor finish the gesture in their own head. Which arms would you give her?

quiz.question: What does “Milo” in the statue's name refer to?
options: The Greek island of Melos where she was found
The French officer who sketched her
quiz.explanation: Milo is a later spelling of Melos, the island where she was dug up in 1820.

quiz.question: What does the roll of drapery around her hips help hide?
options: The joint between two blocks of marble
A crack caused by an earthquake
quiz.explanation: The torso and the legs are separate blocks that meet at the hips.

quiz.question: Why were the arms especially likely to be lost?
options: They were sawn off for transport
They were carved separately and pinned on
quiz.explanation: The arms were add-on pieces held by pegs, the weakest points of the statue.

quiz.question: What object does the marble hand found near her hold?
quiz.explanation: A hand holding an apple was found close to the statue.

quiz.question: What did the lost inscription reveal?
options: That she was made in the Hellenistic period by a sculptor from Antioch
That she was carved in Rome
quiz.explanation: The signature named a sculptor from Antioch on the Maeander, pointing to a later date than the Louvre wanted.

facts.text: The Venus de Milo is about the height of an average woman.
facts.explanation: At 2.04 m (about 6 ft 8 in) she is well over life size.

facts.text: Holes in the marble show she once wore metal jewelry.
facts.explanation: The stone was pierced to attach ornaments such as an armband and earrings.

facts.text: Restorers in the 1820s gave her new arms that were later removed.
facts.explanation: They considered adding arms but decided to leave her as she was found.
